## Abstract

**Background:** NHL First and Second Team All-Stars are awarded by the
PHWA after every season. This project wants to explore the possibility
of predicting these picks using individual player data.

**Data:** The dataset includes 2747 instances of NHL players who played
in seasons between 2018 and 2022 and played at least a quarter of the
season. The data was gathered from hockey-reference.com. Using the base
dataset, variables were created to account for differing season lengths
due to Covid. These variables were the position group (forward or
defenseman), percentage of total games played, and point per game rate.
Interactions between the season and points per game rate and the points
per game rate and position group were explored, but they didn't improve
the predictive power of the model.

**Results:** The model showed a positive relationship between a games
percentage increment up 0.1 and being an All-Star (OR = 3.57), a
positive relationship between a points per game rate increment up 0.1 and
being an All-Star (OR = 4.89), and a negative relationship between being
a forward and being an All-Star (OR = 0.001). The model had an accuracy
around 99% for both the training and testing sets, and its sensitivity
increased from 0.53 in the training set to 0.9 in the testing set. The
model predicted the 2022-23 Second Team to be Leon Draisaitl, Jason
Robertson, Nikita Kucherov, Quinn Hughes, and Dougie Hamilton. It
predicted the 2022-23 First Team to be Connor McDavid, Matthew Tkachuk,
David Pastrnak, Erik Karlsson, and Josh Morrissey.

**Conclusions:** First and Second Team NHL All Stars can be predicted
with moderately decent accuracy based on a individual player
statistics; however there are certain non-statistical factors that might
effect writer voting that can't be accounted for.

## Introduction

After every NHL season, representatives from the Professional Hockey
Writers Association gather to vote on the most outstanding players at
each position. Each writer gets 3 votes per position: one for first
another for second, and one for third. A third place vote is worth 1
point, a second place vote is worth 3, and a first place vote is worth
5. The points are counted up and if a player is a forward and gets the
most points out of all players at their forward position, or a player is
a defenseman and gets top 2 in points among defensemen, they become a
First Team NHL All-Star. The players with the second highest votes at
each forward position and the third and fourth most points as defensemen
are named Second Team NHL All-Stars. Although the names are similar,
these selections shouldn't be mistaken for players who make an All-Star
Game appearance. This honor is the equivalent of the All-NBA teams for
the NBA and the All-MLB teams for the MLB.

The question this project seeks to answer is whether players with the
honor of being a First or Second Team All-Star can be identified using a
that player's individual statistics. I also want to use said predictive
method to predict the players who will earn First and Second Team
All-Star honors for the current 2022-23 season.

## Data

This players dataset features the individual season statistics of NHL
players who played at least a quarter of the games in the 2018-19,
2019-20, 2020-21, and 2021-22 seasons. The data was pulled from
[hockey-reference.com](https://www.hockey-reference.com/leagues/NHL_2022_skaters.html).
The statistics of the original dataset include the age of the player,
the team he played for, the number of games he played, his goals,
assists, and points, his point share value, the number of shots he took,
his shooting percentage, the amount of time he spent on the ice during
the season in minutes, and the season they played in. Due to the 2019-20
and 2020-21 seasons being shortened by the pandemic, I had to create a
few variables to standardize the seasons regardless of their length.

@tbl-code displays a codebook with all the variables considered for the
logistic regression model. All the variables aside from `age`, `season`,
and `pos_group` are examples of variables I created to standardize the
seasons. `pos_group` was created to group together all the forward
positions and defense positions because there isn't statistical
difference among the different forward positions and defense positions,
just between forwards and defensemen.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-code
#| tbl-cap: "Codebook for the First and Second All-NHL Predictive Logistic Regression project"
#| echo: false
codebook <- tribble(
 ~`VARIABLE NAME`, ~DESCRIPTION,
 "age", "age of the player",
 "pos_group", "is the player a forward or a defenseman",
 "games_per", "percentage of the total games in a season the player played",
 "ppg", "points per game rate",
 "season", "the year the player played in (2018, 2019, 2020, 2021)"
)
knitr::kable(codebook)
```

```{r}
GGally::ggpairs(

```

```{r}
#| label: quant-tbl
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| tbl-cap: "Summary Statistics of Quantatative Variables"
var_table <- data.frame(predictor = c("age", "games percentage", "points per game"))
  vars <- favstats(~ age, data = players) |>
  full_join(favstats(~ games_per, data = players)) |>
  full_join(favstats(~ ppg, data = players))
  
var_table <- var_table |>
  bind_cols(vars) |>

knitr::kable(var_table, digits = 2)
```

```{r}

knitr::kable(tally(~ pos_group, data = players))
knitr::kable(tally(~ season, data = players))
knitr::kable(tally(~ all_star_team, data = players))

```

The dataset contains the seasonal individual player data for 2747 total
forwards and defense that played in NHL seasons between 2018 and 2022
who played at least a quarter of the season. 1802 of the 2747 player
seasons were from forwards and 945 were from defensemen. Of those 2747
player seasons, only 40 of those instances earned the player the title
of First or Second Team All-Star. The oldest player to play in the NHL
over this time frame was 44 years old and the youngest player was 18.
Points per game rates ranged from 0 to 1.88. The percentage of games
played ranged from 26.8% to 102.4%. Players who played more than 100% of
total games in a season were players who played all of one teams games
while rostered, got traded to another team that had played less games,
and played the rest of the new team's

The pairs plot (see @fig-pairs) displays the relationship between the
main variables being considered for the logistic regression model
grouped by the response variable `all_star_team`. Red represents
non-all-stars and blue represents the all-stars. Age, points per game,
and point share per game all have a slight right-skew. Games percentage
has a heavy left-skew indicating that a large amount of the players
played near-full seasons. Characteristics of a All-Star player that I
can see from the plots are that they play most of the season and they
have a high points per game rate. Age doesn't appear to be a significant
factor from the univariate distribution in the pairs plot.

Two interactions that were tested for the multiple logistic regression
model are the between `pos_group` and `ppg` and `ppg` and `season`. When
looking pair plot of `pos_group` and `ppg` in @fig-pairs, there's a
discrepancy between the distribution of `ppg` for forwards and
defensemen. This is because defensemen aren't expected to contribute to
a team's offensive output as much of forwards. I though that the model
should take that into account with an interaction. I also wanted to look
into the second interaction, `ppg` and `season`, because scoring has
been on the incline in the NHL over the past few seasons. More players
are getting higher point totals year after year.

```{r}
#| echo: false
null_mod <- glm(all_star_team ~ games_per + pos_group + ppg + season,
family = "binomial", data = players)

interaction_mod <- glm(all_star_team ~ games_per + pos_group + ppg + season + pos_group * ppg + ppg * season,
family = "binomial", data = players)

anova(null_mod, interaction_mod, test = "Chisq")
```

According to the chi-squared test above, with a p-value of 0.79, it
appears that the interactions between `pos_group` and `ppg` and `ppg`
and `season` are not significant in predicting whether a player is an
All-Star.

## Results

### Final Model

```{r}
#| label: tbl-reg
#| tbl-cap: "Multiple Regression Model for the Player Data"
#| echo: false
train <- players |> filter(season != 2021)
test <- players |> filter(season == 2021)

mod_final <- logistic_reg(mode = "classification") |>
  set_engine("glm") |>
  fit(all_star_team ~ games_per10 + pos_group + ppg10  + season, data = train)

cleaned_up <- broom::tidy(mod_final) |>
  rename(`p-value` = p.value) |>
  mutate(
    term = str_replace(term, "pos_group", "Position: "),
    `est (SE)` = paste0(round(estimate, 2), " (", round(std.error, 2), ")"),
    `OR` = round(exp(estimate), 2)
  ) |>
  select(term, `est (SE)`, `OR`, `p-value`)
knitr::kable(cleaned_up, digits = 2)

```

@tbl-reg shows the predictors of the final model. The `games_per`
variable and `ppg` variable were recoded so that interpretations of a
0.1 increase in their values could be made. The percentage of games
played, the points per game rate, and whether the player is a forward or
defenseman have great significance in predicting whether a players is a
First or Second Team NHL All-Star. For every additional 0.1 increase to
`games_per`, a player's odds of being an All-Star increases 3.6 times.
For every additional 0.1 increase to `ppg`, the odds a player is an
All-Star becomes 4.9 times greater. The odds of being an All-Star are
significantly less if the player is a forward rather than a defenseman.
The season a player played in has no statistical significance.

The significance of the the position group of the player may be
attributed to the proportions of players in each group in the entire
dataset versus those who are All-Stars. Defensemen make up 34% of the
dataset, but they make up 40% of non-goalie All-Stars.

Games percentage is incredibly significant in determining who WON'T be
an All-Star. When looking at the univariate distribution of `games_per`
in @fig-pairs, there isn't a single player who played less than 75% of
their games and was an All-Star. Most All-Stars have a `games_per` value
that falls between 0.9 and 1.

Points per game is also a strong predictor which can be observed when
looking at the `ppg` univariate distribution in @fig-pairs as well. The
clear divide in the distributions of All-Stars and non-All-Stars is
apparent.

All these strong predictors combine to create an accurate model.

```{r}
#| echo: false
players <- players |>
  bind_cols(
    predict(mod_final, new_data = players, type = "class"),
    ) |>
  rename(team_prediction = .pred_class)
```



```{r}
#| label: fig-allstars
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| fig-cap: "Plot of players who were All-Stars stratified by season based on games percentage and points per game"
ggplot(data = players, aes(x = games_per10, y = ppg10)) +
  geom_count(
    data = players,
    aes(color = all_star_team), alpha = 0.7
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("red", "blue")) +
  
  facet_wrap(~fct_rev(as.factor(season)))
```
```{r}
#| label: fig-prediction
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| fig-cap: "Plot of players who were predicted to be All-Stars stratified by season based on games percentage and points per game"

ggplot(data = players, aes(x = games_per10, y = ppg10)) +
  geom_count(
    data = players,
    aes(color = team_prediction), alpha = 0.7
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("red", "blue")) +
  
  facet_wrap(~fct_rev(as.factor(season)))
```

@fig-allstars plots All-Stars versus non-All-Stars in the entirety of 
the players dataset based on `ppg` and `games_per`. @fig-prediction 
does the same but plots the final model's predictions instead.
When comparing @fig-allstars and @fig-prediction, the predictions versus 
the actual all-stars are show some consistency. All-Stars tend to have
a high `ppg` and `games_per` which is reflected in both plots. For both 
plots the distributions appear to be the similar regardless of the season.

### Assessing the Model

```{r}
#| echo: false
train <- train |>
  bind_cols(
    predict(mod_final, new_data = train, type = "class"),
    )

test <- test |>
  bind_cols(
    predict(mod_final, new_data = test, type = "class"),
    )

mod_yes <- logistic_reg(mode = "classification") |>
  set_engine("glm") |>
  fit(all_star_team ~ 0, data = train)

mod_no <- logistic_reg(mode = "classification") |>
  set_engine("glm") |>
  fit(all_star_team ~ 1, data = train)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-accuracy
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Model accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity measures for the All-Star Team model"
assess_tbl <- tibble(
model = c("Always", "Never", "Final"),
mod =  list(mod_yes, mod_no, mod_final)
)

assess_tbl <- assess_tbl |>
  mutate(
    y_train = list(pull(train, all_star_team)),
    y_test = list(pull(test, all_star_team)),
    y_hat_train = map(
      mod,
      ~pull(predict(.x, new_data = train, type = "class"), .pred_class)
    ),
    y_hat_test = map(
      mod,
      ~pull(predict(.x, new_data = test, type = "class"), .pred_class)
    )
  )

assess_tbl <- assess_tbl |>
  mutate(
    acc_train = map2_dbl(y_train, y_hat_train, accuracy_vec),
    acc_test = map2_dbl(y_test, y_hat_test, accuracy_vec),
    sens_train = map2_dbl(y_train, y_hat_train, sens_vec, event_level = "second"),
    sens_test = map2_dbl(y_test, y_hat_test, sens_vec, event_level = "second"),
    spec_train = map2_dbl(y_train, y_hat_train, spec_vec, event_level = "second"),
    spec_test = map2_dbl(y_test, y_hat_test, spec_vec, event_level = "second")
    ) |>
  select(-mod, -matches("^y")) |>
  arrange(desc(acc_test))

knitr::kable(assess_tbl, digits = 4)
```

@tbl-accuracy displays the final model's performance with the training
and testing sets when compared to models that either only categorize
players as non-All-Stars or only categorize players as All-Stars. The
training set contained instances of players playing in seasons other
than the 2021-22 season and the testing set contained only the players
of that 2021-22 season. This divide created a 75-25 split.

The final model had higher accuracy in both the training and testing
sets than both the other models. It identified 53% of the All-Stars in
the training set and it did an even better job of identifying All-Stars
in the testing set, getting 90% of them correct. The specificity
decreased from the training set to the testing set (0.998 to 0.989),
however for the purpose of this project, getting slightly more false
positives is not detrimental.

### Predicting the 2022-23 All-Stars

```{r}
#| label: tbl-players
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "15 Players with the Highest Probabilities of being All-Stars"
players2022_head <- players2022 |>
  bind_cols(
    predict(mod_final, new_data = players2022, type = "prob"),
    ) |>
  rename(team_probability = .pred_Yes) |>
  select(player, pos, gp, g, a, pts, team_probability) |>
  arrange(desc(team_probability)) |>
  head(15)

knitr::kable(players2022_head, digits = 4)
```

@tbl-players displays the 15 players who played in the 2022-23 season
with the highest probabilities of being either a First or Second Team
All-Star sorted from highest probability to lowest. A general trend
between the probability and points can be seen when comparing forwards
to forwards and defensemen to defensemen.

#### 2022-23 Second Team All-Stars

**C - Leon Draisaitl, Edmonton Oilers, #29, Probability: 99.7%**

**80 GP - 52 G - 76 A - 128 Pts**

Draisaitl finished the season 4th in goals and 2nd in total points.

**LW - Jason Robertson, Dallas Stars, #21, Probability: 84.9%**

**82 GP - 46 G - 63 A - 109 Pts**

Roberston was tied for 6th in points this season.

**RW - Nikita Kucherov, Tampa Bay Lightning, #86, Probability: 92.4%**

**82 GP - 30 G - 83 A - 113 Pts**

Kucherov was 3rd in points and 2nd in assists among all players
this season.

**D - Quinn Hughes, Vancouver Canucks, #43, Probability: 89.7%**

**78 GP - 7 G - 69 A - 76 Pts**

Hughes was tied for second in points among defensemen. He also finished
second in assists among defensemen.

**D - Dougie Hamilton, New Jersey Devils, #7, Probability: 83.9%**

**78 GP - 22 G - 52 A - 74 Pts**

Hamilton finished 2nd in league for goals scored by defensemen.

#### 2022-23 First Team All-Stars

**C - Connor McDavid, Edmonton Oilers, #97, Probability: 100%**

**82 GP - 64 G - 89 A - 153 Pts**

McDavid led the league in goals with 64 and was the first player since
Mario Lemieux in 1996 to eclipse 150 points in a season.

**LW - Matthew Tkachuk, Florida Panthers, #19, Probability: 88.7%**

**79 GP - 40 G - 69 A - 109 Pts**

Tkachuk finished the season tied for 6th in points. His exceptional
performance in the regular season dragged his Florida team to a Wild
Card placement in the playoffs.

**RW - David Pastrnak, Boston Bruins, #88, Probability: 92.4%**

**82 GP - 61 G - 52 A - 113 Pts**

Pastrnak became one of only 5 players to score over 60 goals in a season
in the 21st century.

**D - Erik Karlsson, San Jose Sharks, #65, Probability: 99.9%**

**82 GP - 25 G - 76 A - 101 Pts**

Karlsson is the first defenseman since Brian Leech in 1992 to score over
100 points in a season.

**D - Josh Morrissey, Winnipeg Jets, #44, Probability: 89.7%**

**78 GP - 16 G - 60 A - 76 Pts**

Morrissey tied for 2nd in points among all defensemen.

## Conclusion

The goal of this project was to create a model that can accurately
predict the future First and Second Team NHL All-Stars. Through the
created model, I found that there was a positive association between a
high games played percentage and a high points per game rate and being
an All-Star, and a negative association between being a forward and
being an All-Star. The develop logistic regression model made successful
predictions in both the training and testing sets, having an accuracy of
around 99% for both, and a higher true positive rate (sensitivity) for
the testing set than the training set. I'm also pleased with the model's
picks for the 2022-23 NHL All-Star Teams.

There are some limitations for the model. It can't account for
non-statistical factors that influence the writers decisions when
casting their votes. For example, despite them being the top 2 players
in points this season, some writers might not vote for both Connor
McDavid and Leon Draisaitl because they play for the same team at the
same position. This happened in the 2020-21 season, when Draisaitl was
the First Team Center thanks to an incredible goal-scoring pace in the
season, but McDavid, despite having the most points that season (and the
highest point per game rate out of any instance in the dataset), didn't
even get a nod for the Second Team Center position. Creating a
categorical variable that would deal with this situation (whether a
teammate at a players position was an All-Star or not) wouldn't be
possible for predicting future events, because it's dependent on the
response variable.

Possible improvements for the model could include adding a goals per
game rate. The issue with that variable is that there is definitely
multicollineary with point share, which most likely means there's
correlation with points per game rate. I also looked at the top scorers
of the 2022-23 season and my feeling is that while I think that the top
few goal scorers might have a chance, players that score goals and don't
get as many assists don't look amazing candidates. The goal scorer has
to be scoring at a rate the sets them apart from the rest.
